title: Separated growth of Bi-Cu bimetallic electrocatalysts on defective copper foam for highly converting CO2 to formate with alkaline anion-exchange membrane beyond KHCO3 electrolyte
abstract: Tuning the geometric and electronic structure of bimetallic electrocatalyst to facilitate a specific reaction pathway and offer more active sites is a promising avenue for enhancing activity and selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR). Owing to formation of Bi-Cu interface through the separated growth of Bi and Cu atoms on defective copper foam, the Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode converts CO2 to formate with an allured Faradaic efficiency (94.37%) and partial current density (27.85 mA cm 2) at -0.91 Vversus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Notably, such electrode with tight moss-like structure delivers the excellent durability under 58 h electrolysis, outperforming most of the current Bi-based catalysts. Moreover, we have experimentally shown that KOH is a better electrolyte than KHCO3 due to the lower solution resistance and more confinement of free CO2 gas, and the alkaline anion-exchange membrane is more ideal than the cation-exchange membrane counterpart, owing to the enhancement of formate selectivity by suppressing the evolution of H2. This study inspires a complete set of concepts for highly converting CO2 to formate that contains the design of effective electrocatalysts, the role of growth substrate, the effect of different electrolytes and membranes.

Separated growth of Bi-Cu bimetallic electrocatalysts on defective copper foam for highly converting CO2 to formate with alkaline anion-exchange membrane beyond KHCO3 electrolyte
Luwei Peng a, Yaofeng Wang a, Yongxia Wang a, Nengneng Xu c, Wenshuang Lou a, Peixuan Liu a, Dongqing Cai a, Haitao Huang d, Jinli Qiao a,b,* a State Key Laboratory for Modification of Chemical Fibers and Polymer Materials, College of Environmental Science and Engineering, Shanghai 201620, PR China b Shanghai Institute of Pollution Control and Ecological Security, Shanghai 200092, PR China c Department of Chemical Engineering, Institute for Materials Research and Innovation, University of Louisiana at Lafayette, Lafayette, LA, 70504, United States d Department of Applied Physics, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, 11 YucaiRoad, Kowloon, Hongkong, China
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode KOH and KHCO3 Alkaline anion-exchange membrane
A B S T R A C T
Tuning the geometric and electronic structure of bimetallic electrocatalyst to facilitate a specific reaction pathway and offer more active sites is a promising avenue for enhancing activity and selectivity of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction (eCO2RR). Owing to formation of Bi-Cu interface through the separated growth of Bi and Cu atoms on defective copper foam, the Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode converts CO2 to formate with an allured Faradaic efficiency (94.37%) and partial current density (27.85 mA cm− 2) at -0.91 Vversus reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). Notably, such electrode with tight moss-like structure delivers the excellent durability under 58 h electrolysis, outperforming most of the current Bi-based catalysts. Moreover, we have experimentally shown that KOH is a better electrolyte than KHCO3 due to the lower solution resistance and more confinement of free CO2 gas, and the alkaline anion-exchange membrane is more ideal than the cation-exchange membrane counterpart, owing to the enhancement of formate selectivity by suppressing the evolution of H2. This study inspires a complete set of concepts for highly converting CO2 to formate that contains the design of effective electrocatalysts, the role of growth substrate, the effect of different electrolytes and membranes.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
The rising CO2 concentration in atmosphere results in numerous environmental issues (the increase of global temperature and the unpleasant climate change) [1]. In order to alleviate environmental problems, the technologies of CO2 conversion containing microbial electrosynthesis [2], photocatalytic reduction [3], solid oxide electrolysis [4], and electrochemical reduction have been put forward successively [5]. Among these strategies, converting CO2 into high value-added fuels and chemical feedstocks by a benign electrochemical method can not only availably utilize the intermittent sources of energy such as solar and wind energies, but also realize a carbon cycle by moving the carbon species from one reservoir (CO2) to another [6]. Furthermore, the electrochemical CO2 reduction reactions (eCO2RR) as half-cathode reaction can combine with other anode reactions to achieve a system of metal− CO2 batteries [7], or pure oxygen evolution cell
[8], which can enhance the overall energy efficiency. One of the biggest challenges to deploy eCO2RR is that CO2, as a thermodynamically stable linear molecule, inescapably induces the sluggish reaction kinetic and low electrochemical activity [9]. To tackle this hurdle, it has been proved that numerous noble (Au [10], Ag [11], Pd [12]) and non-noble (Sn [13], Bi [14], In [15], Cu [16], Co [17]) metals show enhanced performance of eCO2RR. Intriguingly, noble metals and Co, on the one hand, are generally treated as the best candidates for the production of carbon monoxide, while on the other hand, Sn, Bi and In show the excellent activity of formate generation. Meanwhile, Cu with unavoidable hydrogen evolution reaction in aqueous electrolyte, has demonstrated the potential to produce multiple hydrocarbon with low selectivity [18]. However, most of single metal catalysts suffer from high cost, inferior electroconductivity and low selectivity. Consequently, how to develop the cost-effective electrocatalyst of eCO2RR with high current density, moderate selectivity and outstanding stability at low

overpotential for future practical application, is still a big challenge to accomplish.
As the synergistic effect in binary or multicomponent electrocatalyst has been affirmed to promote a specific catalytic reaction [19], reasonably designing the synergistic effect of bimetallic catalyst for eCO2RR is an effective and potential approach to enhance the activity, selectivity and stability by controlling both the geometric and electronic structure of local environments [20], which definitely affects the reaction mechanism and selectivity of targeted production [21]. By introducing Bi nanoparticles into SnO2 nanosheets to form a Sn-Bi interface with orbital interactions, the Sn-Bi interface favors the adsorption of OCHO* intermediate and facilitates the electron transfer to the adsorption CO2, thus promoting the conversion of CO2 to formate with remarkable stability and selectivity [20]. It is not a unique instance, but has its counterpart. For Bi-doped SnO nanosheets, Bi doping can enhance the adsorption of OCHO* intermediates and protect the divalent tin from being reduced metallic tin [22]. Besides, Bi-modified Zn catalyst with bimetallic interfaces and grain boundaries can stabilize the OCHO* intermediates, leading to a higher selectivity and activity for the production of formate [21].
Except Bi as an electron and microstructure regulator, Cu element has shown its promising potential for eCO2RR that is validated by Matthew W. Kanan [23], although the existing challenges (favorable H2 evolution, low energy efficiency and selectivity toward targeted production) cannot be neglected [24]. One attractive way to address these dilemmas is that Cu as a secondary metal combines with another metallic substrate to regulate the reaction pathways of CO2 intermediates and the distribution of specific production. By a facile coprecipitation method, Cu mixed with indium can form a core–shell structure that tunes the distribution of CO and HCOOH by affecting the binding energies of intermediates [25]. The incorporation of Cu into Sn materials can boost the electron transfer from Sn to Cu, ensuring that Sn stays at positive oxidation states, thereby suppressing hydrogen and CO generation and promoting formate selectivity [26]. Coincidentally, the heterogeneous Cu is doped into Bi nanocrystals to modulate the local electronic environment of Bi atoms, thus altering the formation pathway of OCHO* intermediate and prohibiting the formation of by-products CO and H2 [27]. In a word, Bismuth, as an environmentally benign and less toxic metal compared with its neighbors in the periodic table, is a soft metal in texture and its electronic conductivity is also low. Therefore, reconstructing the intrinsic and electronic structure of Bi metal to a stable state by incorporating Cu atom is a compelling protocol to enhance the activity and selectivity of converting CO2 to formate, according to the adsorption of favorable intermediates and the synergistic effect on the surface of binary metal. It is generally believed that mesoporous and nanoporous metallic structures are very attractive due to the high surface area and large pore volume, which is favorable for mass transport of reactants and exposure of active sites [28–30]. Inspiringly, the electrochemical deposition technique is an effective method to precisely control the nanoporous architecture (i.e., pore size, surface area, pore structure, etc.) of electrode materials [31].
Herein, we have synthesized a bimetallic electrocatalyst with separated growth of Bi and Cu atoms on the defective copper foam via a facile electrochemical deposition method for highly efficient conversion of formate. The synergistic effect of Bi and Cu atom along with a tight moss-like structure favors the adsorption of OCHO* intermediate, resulting in a superb durability (58 h) and high partial current density toward formate (27.85 mA cm− 2). Speficically, the defective copper foam as a growth substrate to deposit Cu and Bi atoms has a more positive effect to form a stable deposition structure than the pristine copper foam. Based on the analysis of different electrolytes and membranes, the strong alkaline electrolyte (KOH) illustrates better activity than KHCO3 due to the lower solution resistance and more confinement of free CO2 gas in KOH, and the alkaline anion-exchange membrane is a more ideal separator than the cation-exchange membrane counterpart, owing to the enhancement of formate selectivity by suppressing the
evolution of H2.

sections.heading: 2.1. Materials
sections.text: Trisodium citrate dehydrate (Na3C6H5O7 2H2O, ≥99%), Ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (C10H16N2O8, ≥99.5%), Urea (CH4N2O, ≥99%), Bismuth nitrate pentahydrate (Bi(NO3)3 5H2O, ≥99%), Copper nitrate trihydrate (Cu(NO3)2 3H2O, ≥99%) were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co. Ltd, China without further purification. Sodium formate (CHNaO2, ≥99.5%) was purchased from Aladdin Industrial Corporation. The pristine copper foam and copper foil were purchased from Kunshan Guangjiayuan new materials Co. Ltd and were introduced oxygen defects on the surface by immersing them into 0.1 M H2SO4 and acetone for 30 min, and after that for 120 ◦C heat treatment 1 h in air condition. The bore diameter and porosity of copper foam is 0.1 mm–10 mm (5− 120ppi) and 50%–98%, respectively. The open-holes ratio and bulk density of pristine copper foam is ≥98% and 0.1− 0.8 g/cm3, respectively. The alkaline anion-exchange membrane (FAA-3PK-130) was purchased from Fuel Cell Store.

sections.heading: 2.2. Fabrication of Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode
sections.text: The Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode was obtained by a simple and one-step co-electrodeposition method via applying hydrogen bubble template [32]. 2.941 g Na3C6H5O7 2H2O (0.01 mol) and 0.6 g CH4N2O were mixed with 0.594 g C10H16N2O8 (2 μmol) in 100 mL deionized water stirring for complete dissolution. Then 0.97 g Bi(NO3)3 5H2O (2 μmol), 0.0805 g Cu(NO3)3 3H2O (0.333 μmol) and 0.68 g CHNaO2 (10 μmol) were added in the mentioned clear solution, which was stirred to a transparent solution and then sonicated for 30 min. The Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode was fabricated by applying two electrode system, wherein the spectral graphite carbon wire was employed as counter electrode and the pre-treatment copper foam cut into a piece of 1.5*1 cm2 was employed as working electrode. The seperate growth of Cu and Bi atoms was achieved by the co-electrodeposition method in a high constant current density (400 mA) for 1 min. The obtained Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode was rinsed for several times with deionized water before CO2 performance test.

sections.heading: 2.3. Fabrication of pure Cu or Bi electrode
sections.text: The only Cu or Bi electrode was obtained by the same mentioned method. The difference was the plating solution. The only Cu plating solution did not contain the Bi(NO3)3 5H2O and C10H16N2O8 while the only Bi plating solution did not contain the Cu(NO3)3 3H2O compared with Cu/Bi plating solution.

sections.heading: 2.4. Materials characterization
sections.text:
The crystal structures of samples were detected by a Philips PW3830 X-ray diffractometer at 40 mA and 40 kV by using Cu Ka radiation (l = 1.5406 Å). For conforming the indices of crystallographic plane, the jade 6 software was used to fit the standard PDF card. The chemical and electronic states of samples were analyzed by a spectrometer (RBDupgraded PHI-5000C ECSA system (PerkinElmer) with an Al Ka X-ray anode source (hν = 1486.6 eV). In order to avoid the oxidation of the samples, these samples were always served in an airtight container with the protection of N2 before the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements. All the binding energies (C1 s, Cu2p, Bi4f, O1 s) were calibrated by using the standard C1 s binding energy peak (284.8 eV) as a reference and the fitting peaks of Cu2p, Bi4f and O1 s were added and optimized by using XPSpeak software. The morphology of as-prepared electrodes was investigated by a S-4800 field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM) operating at 5 kV. Samples for SEM were cut into
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
small pieces and then stuck on the specimen holder by using a conductive tape. A high-resolution Hitachi JEM-2100 F was operated at 200 kV to observe the detail morphology of the obtained electrode. The element distribution was determined by an energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) at 10 kV. Samples for Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analyses were firstly immersed in ethanol for 30 min under ultrasound treatment, after that using a rubber head dropper to drop several droplets on a 200 mesh molybdenum grids with the assist of lamp irradiation.

sections.heading: 2.5. Electrochemical performance of CO2 reduction
sections.text:
All the electrochemical performance of CO2 reduction was carried out by a workstation (CHI 760E, Shanghai Chenhua) in a typical H-cell, where the anodic and cathodic compartments were separated by a membrane to prevent the CO2 reduction productions from cathodic compartment to anodic compartment. In anodic compartment, a 0.5 M KOH was conducted as anolyte for oxygen evolution reaction and the spectral graphite carbon was conducted as counter electrode. In cathodic compartment, the catholyte utilized in this work was 0.5 M KHCO3 and KOH to investigate the influence of electrolyte and the Ag/ AgCl was used as reference electrode. The working electrode with effective area (1*1 cm2) was carried out for the electrochemical performance. Before each specific experiment, the catholyte was purged with N2 and CO2 for 30 min, and the pH of 0.5 M KHCO3 saturated with N2 and CO2 was 8.3 and 7.4, while the pH of 0.5 M KOH saturated with N2 and CO2 was 12.4 and 9.5. All the mentioned potentials in this work were relative to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) by the following Eq. (1):
E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.197 + 0.0591 ∗ pH (1)

sections.heading: 2.6. Products analysis
sections.text:
Liquid products were analyzed by an Ion Chromatography (IC1820, Shanghai Sunny Hengping Scientific instrument Co. Ltd). The precolumn (IC SI-90 G No. J38J0065) and chromatographic column (IC SI-90 4E No. G1920020) were installed on the IC1820. In addition, an Anion Suppressor (AES-100) was mounted on the IC 1820 to effectively reduce background conductance and improve the tested sensitivity. Prior to injection, the liquid samples were diluted for 5, 10 or 20 times with purified water. Considering one CO2 molecule converted to formate transfers two electrons, the Faradaic efficiency towards formate is given as following Eq. (2):
FEHCOO− (%) = 2 ∗ n ∗ F
Q (2)
Where 2 is the electron transferred number of one CO2 molecule to HCOO− , F is the Faraday constant (F = 96,485 C mol-1), n is the produced mole of HCOO− , Q is the total charge passed across the working electrode (Q = I*t).
Gas products were analyzed by the in-situ online Gas Chromatography (GC-2014C, Shimadzu), which was equipped with TCD-2014C and FID-2014C. The carrier gas was argon and the standard gas sample including 1.00% CH4, 0.51% C2H6, 0.50% C2H4, 2.02% CO, 1.06% H2 and the rest of gas (N2), was applied to get the standard curve that quantified the content of gas productions. The CO2-flow rate was controlled by a gas flowmeter. Prior to inject the product gas, a Complete Filter Bundle Kit was used to dehumidify the gas sample. The Faradaic efficiency of gas products is given as following Eq. (3):
FEgas(%) = v 60 s/min ∗ c 24000 cm3mol ∗ N ∗ F
jtotal = 0.067 ∗ v ∗ c ∗ N jtotal
(3)
Where N is the electron transferred number of one CO2 molecule to H2/ CO or other gas products, v is the CO2 flow rate measured by a gas
flowmeter and c is the volume concentration of H2/CO from gas outlet of H-cell.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis of bimetallic Cu and Bi electrode
sections.text:
It can be seen from Fig. 1that the bimetallic Bi-Cu electrode was synthesized by a two-step procedure. Firstly, the thermal treatment of pristine copper foam was at 120 ◦C for 1 h in air condition. As shown from scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images (Fig. 2a), the pristine copper foam distributes a large number of interconnected holes, which would provide enough space to let electrolyte circulate freely. Additionally, the surface of copper foam is fairly smooth (Fig. 2b). The pretreatment of growth substrate is a prerequisite for a successful electrodeposition process, since the first layer of metal deposition determines the binding force between deposited layer and the substrate. After the heat treatment (Fig. 2c), the oxidized copper foam possesses some oxygen defects for the growth of Cu2+ and Bi3+ ion. For better understanding the role of substrate in the growth of Cu2+ and Bi3+, the copper foam was replaced by copper foil to study the substrate effect on the growth. The defective copper foil was thermally treated under the same procedure as that for the defective copper foam. As shown in Figure S1a, when the pristine copper foil is used as a growth substrate to deposit Cu and Bi atom, there is a clear boundary between the growth substrate and deposited layer. Therefore, the initial deposited layer with loose structure is near the boundary, which is lethal for a stable structure. Whilst for the defective copper foil (Figure S1b),the initial deposited layer and growth substrate show a very tight structure, indicating that the thermal treatment of growth substrate has a significant role in the formation of initial deposited layer. Actually, the deposited layer on pristine copper foil manifests a disordered and multi-porous structure in Figure S1c. Instead, the deposited layer on defective copper foam represents a layered and compact structure in Figure S1d, which obviously illustrates that the pre-treatment of growth substrate would also affect the whole microstructure of deposited layer. Besides the difference from the cross section of deposited layer, the superficial morphology of deposited layer also demonstrates a disordered and rough surface on pristine copper foil in Figure S1e but an ordered and smooth surfacein Figure S1f.
Secondly, the Cu and Bi atoms were strongly anchored on the defective copper foam by electrodeposition method at high constant current (400 mA), which allowed Cu and Bi to vertically grow by using hydrogen bubble template for producing three dimensional and hierarchical porous microstructure [32]. It is noteworthy that, this self-assembly of Cu and Bi bimetallic electrode did not use any polymeric binders and any extra conductive additives, such as nafion or graphite, which usually would cause the unwanted interface, limited active sites, substantial proportion of dead volumes, uncontrollable microstructure that lower the overall mass transport and electronic conductivity [33].
As shown in Fig. 2d and Figure S2a,b, the pure Cu dendrite with the stems around 0.27 μm forming a jungle, was successfully deposited on the defective substrate. The plausible mechanism of Cu dendrite formation may be as follows: (i) there will be a depletion zone formed around the growth substrate, when the Cu2+ ion diffusion rate is lower than the deposition rate, (ii) in the depletion zone, the apexes of polyhedral crystal gets into the region of higher Cu2+ ion concentration, and thus grows faster than the central part of the facets [34]. The SEM images (Fig. 2e and Figure S2c,d) of pure Bi electrode show the similar microstructure as pure Cu electrode along with some dendritic crystals and micro cavities (bore diameter: 1.0–1.5 μm) running through inside and outside. Since the standard electrode potentials of Cu2+ (0.324 VSHE) and Bi3+ (0.308 VSHE) are similar, it is very possible that Cu and Bi could mutually grow onto each other with strong interaction to form the bimetallic grains [35]. By adding Cu2+ and Bi3+ ions together into
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
electroplating solution, the Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode (Fig. 2f and Figure S3) displays a tight moss-like microstructure, which is quite different from pure Cu and Bi morphology. This result supports the conclusion that with the introduction of Cu atom during the Bi growth process, there would be the formation of more stable structure due to the disappearance of dendritic crystals and the appearance of bimetallic grains. This moss-like microstructure may provide numerous volumes and active sites to prompt the mass transfer of CO2 reaction
intermediate, thus facilitating the eCO2RR [36]. To investigate the crystallographic information of the as-prepared electrodes, X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of pure Cu electrode in Fig. 2g shows the typical peaks at 43.47◦, 50.37◦, 73.99◦, indicating the (111), (200), (220) planes of metal Cu (JCPDS PDF# 01–1241), whereas the pure Bi electrode in Fig. 2h shows three peaks at 27.42◦, 38.27◦, 39.86◦, corresponding to the (012), (104), (110) planes of metal Bi (JCPDS PDF# 01− 0699). However, the pure Bi electrode also shows the
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
typical Cu diffraction peaks due to the high intensity of Cu substrate. The XRD pattern of bimetallic electrode (Fig. 2i) clearly shows the (012) and (110) planes of metallic Bi and the (111), (200), (220) planes of metallic Cu only, which confirms that Cu and Bi atoms are separately grown onto each other forming a stable morphology.
The transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was applied to further observe the microstructure of the as-prepared electrodes. Fig. 3a and Figure S4a,b of pure Cu electrode show a tree-like morphology with some branches along the same direction, which supports the evidence that the crystal growth is mainly along the Cu (111) plane. From the high resolution TEM (Figure S4c), the lattice spacing is 0.2107 nm, which corresponds to the Cu (111) plane. In comparison, pure Bi electrode shows the similar microstructure to pure Cu electrode, while the difference lies in that the branches of Bi electrode are along different directions (Figure S5a,b). More interestingly, the branches of pure Bi electrode are composed of a thick backbone wrapped with a filmy bismuth layer, with some scattered Bi nanoparticles inside (Fig. 3b and Figure S5c). As shown in Figure S5d, thelattice spacing of 0.3192 nm corresponds to the Bi (012) plane, which can be further proved by the inserted fast fourier transformation (FFT) image. However, by adding Cu2+ into the Bi electroplating solution (molar ratio, Cu2+ : Bi3+ = 1 : 6), the as-synthesized Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode with numerous conjunct nano particles shows different morphology neither with pure Cu electrode nor Bi electrode (Figure S6). This distinctive morphology can provide numerous active sites for prompting eCO2RR and vast space for accelerating the diffusion of CO2 intermediate products (Fig. 3c). Fig. 3d shows elemental mapping images of bimetallic electrode where the Bi and Cu atoms are uniformly distributed.Surprisingly, from the mixed picture of Bi and Cu atoms, Cu atoms are found sprinkling evenly on the surface of Bi atoms, which may confirm the separated growth of Cu and Bi atom. Fig. 3e depicts a vivid model of this separated growth of Cu and Bi atom. From high resolution TEM of bimetallic electrode (Fig. 4a,b), a lattice spacing of 0.3275 nm indicates the Bi (012) plane which can be
affirmed by (FFT) image (Fig. 4c), wherein the Bi (012) plane has the highest responding intensity than Cu (111) and (200) planes. Besides, Fig. 4d shows that the weight percentage (wt%) of Cu and Bi is 1:7.785 and the atomic percent (σ) of that is 1:3.
To authenticate the separated growth of Bi and Cu atoms, Bi and Cu atoms were sequentially grown onto each other by placing the growth substrate into pure Bi3+ and Cu2+ electroplating solution in sequence. Firstly, the oxidized copper substrate as working electrode was put into pure Bi3+ electroplating solution for the only bismuth deposition during 10 s. As shown in Figure S7a,b, Bi with flower-like microstructure is generated in the initial stage of deposition, and such multi-channels configuration (Figure S7c,d) is possibly due to the rapid deposition of Bi layer accompanied by the vigorous H2 evolution. As the consumption rate of Bi3+ around growth substrate is beyond the diffusion rate of Bi3+ from electroplating solution, the instantaneous lack of Bi3+ would accelerate H2 formation thus the coalescence of small bubbles leading to the formation of large bubbles. Secondly, the 10 s firstly pre-deposited Bi electrode was put into pure Cu2+ electroplating solution for another 10 s deposition of the only Cu. As expected, Figure S8a,b displays dense and grainy architectures with rough branches, which is totally inconsistent with morphology of the 10 s firstly pre-deposited Bi electrode. Except for the difference in morphology, the relation of deposition Cu layer is more closed as the presence of relatively flat surface in Figure S8c, d compared with Figure S7d. Thirdly, by putting the second-step growth Cu electrode into pure Bi3+ electroplating solution for other 10 s Bi deposition, Figure S9 manifests the same flower-like microstructure with Figure S7. The biggest distinction is the less appearance of multi-channels and the existence of grainy chunks, attributing to the influence of Cu grainy architectures in the second-step electrodeposition. Fourthly, by putting the third-step growth Bi electrode into pure Cu2+ electroplating solution again for the last 10 s deposition, Figure S10 shows almost the same moss-like morphology with the Figure S3, which strongly provides evidence for the separation growth
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
of Cu and Bi atom even in their co-existence solution. To further prove this mechanism, by controlling the molar ratio of Cu2+ and Bi3+ to 6:1, the microstructure of as-obtained bimetallic electrode in Figure S11 is similar to Figure S3, except that Fig S11 shows a higher degree of grainy agglomeration. The above mentioned evidence demonstrates that the concentration of each Cu2+ or Bi3+ in electroplating solution can mutually affect the morphology of deposit.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was employed to explore the chemical states of the as-prepared electrodes. As shown in Cu spectrum (Figure S12), the pure Cu electrode shows two sharp peaks at 932.16 and 951.99 eV, which are ascribed to metallic Cu or Cu+ of the Cu foam substrate [37]. However, the pure Bi and bimetallic electrodes show the same peak positions at 932.16 and 951.99 eV, due to the less content of deposited Cu compared with the copper substrate. Fig. 4e shows that the pure Bi electrode has two strong peaks at 158.80 and 164.12 eV ascribed to Bi3+, suggesting the formation of oxidized surface [38]. The reason could be the exposure in air before the XPS measurements or the adsorbed oxygen. After introducing Cu atom into Bi electrode, the binding energies of Bi 4f7/2 and Bi 4f5/2 has a slightly negative shift (0.12 eV) to 158.68 and 164.00 eV, clearly indicating the electron transfer from Cu to Bi. This electron transfer will reconstruct the electric field of active sites, thereby forming a Bi-Cu interface to synergistically promote the CO2 reduction [39]. The CV curves of bimetallic electrode in Figure S13 shows a positive shift (0.045 VRHE) to 0.163 VRHE compared with pure Bi electrode, also demonstrating that the Cu atom is successfully introduced into Bi species. In addition, the Bi 4f XPS spectra in Fig. 4e of bimetallic electrode after 25 h CO2 electroreduction shows a positive shift (0.16 and 0.37 eV) to 158.96 and 164.49 eV, indicating electron transfer from Bi to the other species possibly due to the formation of bismuth hydroxide, which can be observed from the O 1s
spectra (Figure S14). In Figure S14, there are only one dominant peaks at 531.00 eV indicating the Bi− OH lattice after CO2RR. Meanwhile, the atomic percentage of oxygen (80.33%) after eCO2RR is higher than the percentage (70.88%) before eCO2RR (Table S1), which also supports the formation of bismuth hydroxide.

sections.heading: 3.2. Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2
sections.text:
For eliminating the effect of oxidized surface, the as-prepared electrodes were tested by the in-situ pre-reduction process using chronoamperometry method at -0.6 VRHE in N2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 for 30 min. Subsequently, the electrocatalytic activities of bimetallic electrode (Fig. 5a), pure Bi and Cu electrodes (Figure S15) were measured by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) at 5 mV/s. Fig. 5a and Figure S15 show that the current density in CO2-saturated condition is larger than N2-saturated condition, demonstrating that all of these electrodes are active for CO2 reduction. It is worth noting that the bimetallic electrode shows a potential of -0.85 VRHE at 10 mA cm− 2 in CO2-saturated condition compared with -1.01 VRHE in N2-saturated condition. This reduced potential in CO2 and N2-saturated condition at the same current density demonstrates the better electrocatalytic activity of bimetallic electrode. In addition, the fixed resistance of bimetallic electrode keeps the same both in N2 and CO2-saturated condition, while the charge transfer resistance of the latter has a tremendous decrease compared to the former (Figure S16a), which also demonstrates that Bi-Cu bimetallic electrodes are very active for CO2 reduction. To get insight into the reaction mechanism of eCO2RR, Tafel slopes are derived from Fig. 5b, where the slope values of pure Cu and bimetallic electrode are 138.21 and 138.04 mV per decade near 118 mV per decade. These values demonstrate that the first electron transferring to form an adsorbed
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
CO2*- intermediate is the chemical rate-determining step for CO2 reduction [27]. It has been reported that the surface of pure Bi is favorable for the formation of a COOH* intermediate in Figure S17, which will boost the generation of CO gas [21]. By introducing Cu atoms together with Bi, the intrinsic and electronic structure of Bi electrode will be modulated, thus the reaction pathway of CO2 reduction on Cu and Bi surface will be changed to the formation of OCHO* intermediate, which is regarded as the significant foundation to produce formate (Figure S17). Therefore, the separated growth of Cu and Bi atoms would have a synergistic effect to seize the free CO2 molecule in the electrolyte, then convert to an adsorbed CO2*- intermediate (Fig. 3e), which favors the formation of OCHO* intermediate and prompts the generation of formate by this way.
The product distribution is analyzed at different selected potentials between -0.71 to -1.16 VRHE as shown in Fig. 5c. Bimetallic electrode in 0.5 M KHCO3 with the increasing potential shows that FEHCOO− is discovered to continuously increase in a potential window between -0.71 to -0.91 VRHE, reaching a maximum (95.8%) and then slightly decrease between -0.91 to -1.16 VRHE. This excellent selectivity of formate (FEHCOO− , 95.8%) has surpassed the recently published papaers in eCO2RR [40–43]. Whilst CO and H2 are the only gaseous products and no other gaseous species can be detected by on-line Gas Chromatography (GC). It can be obviously observed that the sum of FECO and FEH2 occupies the dominant position at -0.71 and -0.76 VRHE, then sharply
reduces to no more than 5%. Besides, the total current density enhances from -1.78 mA cm-2at -0.71 VRHE to 58.43 mA cm-2at -1.16 VRHE (Fig. 5d), which is attributed to the rapid reduction of charge transfer resistance along the augment of applied potentials (Figure S16b). Such excellent selectivity and total current density can be concluded by the reasons that the hierarchical moss-like morphology from SEM (Fig. 2f) can provide rough surface, edge and low coordinate sites, resulting in the promotion of eCO2RR. Instead, the pure Cu and Bi electrodes also show the activity of eCO2RR at a certain extent, unfortunately the FEHCOO− is no more than 60% at all selected potential (Figure S18).
As the stability of electrodes for eCO2RR is an important factor to evaluate the future practical application, the stability of Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode is determined in 0.5 M KHCO3 at -0.91 VRHE by using an alkaline anion-exchange membrane (FAA-3-PK-130) to separate the anode and cathode chamber. It can be seen from Fig. 5e that the partial current density of formate (16.03 mA cm− 2) and FEHCOO- (95.8%) slightly oscillate due to the evaporation of formic acid following the CO2 flow and the augment of formic concentration in the electrolyte [44]. For depressing these effects, the electrolyte (0.5 M KHCO3) is refreshed after 25 h electrolysis. It is generally believed that the micro-morphology of electrocatalysts has a relation with the stability of eCO2RR. After 25 h electrolytic reaction, the morphology of bimetallic electrode keeps almost no change in Figure S19, owing to the mutual anchoring effects between Bi and Cu atoms, while the presence of some
L. Peng et al.
Applied Catalysis B: Environmental 288 (2021) 120003
scar can be attributed to the formation of bismuth hydroxide. To further verify the stability of current density, CV curves of bimetallic electrode are tested before the electrolysis, after 25 h and 50 h electrolysis inFig. 5 f. It is as expected that the three curves of current density coincide with each other, which indirectly indicates the good stability of bimetallic electrode.
Electroreduction of CO2 is a system, including the development of electrocatalyst, the design of reactor, the choice of electrolyte and the type of membrane. Unfortunately, most of workers in this field put their efforts on the development of electrocatalyst. In order to wholly understand the eCO2RR, different kinds of electrolytes and membranes are applied in this work. Actually, the electrochemical double layer capacitance (EDLC) has a positive relation with the electrochemical active surface area, which could be used to illustrate the amount of catalytically active sites. As shown in Figure S20, The EDLC of bimetallic electrode in 0.5 M KHCO3 and KOH is 3.12 and 3.52 m F respectively, implying that the active sites of bimetallic electrode in 0.5 M KOH are more than in 0.5 M KHCO3. Indeed, the distribution of production in 0.5 M KOH shows similar trend as in 0.5 M KHCO3, and the FEHCOO− is 94.37% at -0.91 VRHE (Figure S21a). However, the total current density (Figure S21b) in 0.5 M KOH at different selected potentials is largely increased compared to 0.5 M KHCO3 (Fig. 5d) due to the lower solution resistance and more confinement of free CO2 gas. Fig. 5g shows that the charge transfer resistance (R2) in 0.5 M KOH has a huge decrease thus the overall electronic conductivity can be enhanced. These evidences show that KOH is a more ideal electrolyte than KHCO3.
Besides the influence of electrolyte, cation-exchange membrane (Nafion 117) and alkaline anion-exchange membrane (FAA-3-PK-130) are applied to study the performance of eCO2RR by using Bi-Cu bimetallic electrode. As shown in Figure S21c, even though the distribution of production by using Nafion 117 in 0.5 M KHCO3 presents the similar trend as compared to using FAA-3-PK-130 in Fig. 5e, the highest FEHCOO− is only 89.93% at -0.91 VRHE due to the diffusion of H+ from anode to cathode compartment to facilitate the H2 evolution. This can be verified by the increased total current density in Figure S21d and the smaller R2 inFig. 5 g. These evidences show that alkaline anionexchange membrane is a more ideal seperator than cation-exchange membrane. Combined the superiorities of KOH electrolyte and alkaline anion-exchange membrane, the bimetallic electrode as working electrode in 0.5 M KOH using alkaline anion-exchange membrane as a separator, is applied to study the durability in Fig. 5h, where the partial current density of formate has a large enhancement from 16.03–27.85 mA cm-2 at -0.91 VRHE and, the evident fluctuation of current density during 58 h electrolysis possibly due to the relatively faster production of formic acid on the surface of the working electrode. Moreover, the morphology of bimetallic electrode after 25 h electrolysis in 0.5 M KOH (Figure S22) shows some scars on the surface, but no more changes, indicating that the microstructure of the mentioned electrode has a stable nature due to the incorporation of Cu element into Bi species even in the strong alkaline electrolyte. As the selectivity (Faradaic efficiency), activity (partial current density) and durability (electrolysis time) are three important factors to evaluate the performance of eCO2RR for the practical application, this work shows superior performance than most of the state-of-the-art Bi-based eCO2RR catalysts (Fig. 5i and Table S2).

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we have successfully designed a facile and convenient approach to synthetize a bimetallic electrode of Cu-Bi separately grown on each other. Due to the synergistic effect of Cu and Bi atoms, this bimetallic electrode as efficient electrocatalyst for converting CO2 to formate can reach an allured Faradaic efficiency (94.37%) and partial current density (27.85 mA cm− 2) at -0.91 VRHE. Besides, such electrode with tight moss-like structure shows the excellent durability under 58 h electrolysis with no evident degradation in partial current density of formate. Furthermore, the influence of different electrolytes and
membranes reveals that KOH is a more ideal electrolyte than KHCO3 due to the lower solution resistance and more confinement of free CO2 gas, and the alkaline anion-exchange membrane is a more ideal seperator than cation-exchange membrane owing to the enhancement of formate selectivity by suppressing the evolution of H2. This study may provide a deeper concept to directly synthesize the porous bimetallic electrode with synergistic effect via a facile electrochemical deposition method for catalysis, energy storage, conversion reactions and so forth.
